_readme: Chapter 3 keeps Section 3 and its original section numbers; classification pages 1–2 are omitted in this level only.
Section 7 is the single annual table and transfer source. All other terms are optional reading. No client answers appear here.
One blank-line-separated paragraph per value. Simplified classroom exercise; educator review remains pending.

sections.heading: Section 4 – Costs and Purpose
sections.body:
A recorded cost of earning this year's business income. It reduces gross income.

Personal spending does not reduce business income, even with a receipt.

A receipt shows payment. Read its purpose; ask the client if that is unclear.

Ask of every record: Was it earned? Was it for the business? Is it supported? Is it already counted?

sections.heading: Section 5 – Count Once
sections.body:
The same payment may appear on several papers. Count the transaction once.

A bill can support an entry without becoming a second expense.

Compare invoice and order references before adding a payment.

Add each included entry once. Recalculate when an entry changes.

sections.heading: Section 6 – Taxable Income
sections.body:
Supported income before expenses are taken away.

Supported costs of earning that income (Sections 4–5).

Gross income minus allowable expenses. Apply the annual table to this amount, not to gross income.

sections.heading: Section 7 – Annual bands (2023 onwards)
sections.body:
No tax.

15% of the excess over 250,000.

22,500 plus 20% of the excess over 400,000.

102,500 plus 25% of the excess over 800,000.

402,500 plus 30% of the excess over 2,000,000.

2,202,500 plus 35% of the excess over 8,000,000.

Use annual taxable income. Each range excludes its lower limit and includes its upper limit; the first includes zero.

sections.heading: Section 8 – Base Plus Excess
sections.body:
Taxable income minus the band's floor gives the excess.

Multiply only the excess by the band's rate.

Add the band's base tax. Round the finished tax due to cents.

Example: Practice Design Studio has 350,000 taxable income. Excess: 100,000 over 250,000. At 15%, that is 15,000 tax due; base tax is zero.

sections.heading: Section 9 – Credit Versus Expense
sections.body:
An allowable expense reduces income before tax is calculated.

Tax withheld is already paid for the payee. Its certificate identifies the payer, payee, period and amounts.

Tax due minus tax credits equals remaining payable. Example: 15,000 − 2,000 = 13,000. Keep a negative balance's sign.

Use tax withheld for this payee and year. The certificate's income payment is already in the income records; never add it again.

sections.heading: Section 10 – Checking a Computation
sections.body:
Check sources, taxable income, annual band, tax due, credits, then balance. Fix the earliest error first.

Ready means every line is supported and current. This review does not file a return or pay tax.

Use Not Ready while a line needs work. Check it again before requesting approval.

Changing a stamped sheet makes the stamp outdated. Stamp the current version before hand-in.

sections.heading: Section 11 – Explaining the Client Copy
sections.body:
Point to the amount still payable after credits, then explain what it means.

Tax due is the whole tax. Withheld tax is a payment toward it; the remaining balance is what is left.

Keep the approved copy with the records that support it. An unexplained difference is a reason to check, not proof of intent.
